title: Database CPU high and slow user pages
executive_summary: Postgres CPU rose from ~35% to ~64% mean (max 96%) starting 12:45, and user-service p95 latency went from ~80ms to ~1.9s with error rate rising from 0.4% to ~5% from 12:46-12:47. Request rate was flat (~496 rps), so this is not a traffic surge. One change preceded the incident: feature flag feature.profile_v2_cache was enabled on user-service at 12:10 (OPS-2229), which the service logs describe as producing cached payloads ~4.1x larger. Cache-miss fallbacks to the DB begin at 12:45, coinciding with the CPU onset, and the slow statements are the user-profile lookup SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=$1 (22-30s durations). The likely chain is: larger cached payloads -> cache pressure/misses -> profile reads hitting Postgres -> DB saturation -> user-service timeouts. The DBA's 'bad query' theory is not well supported: the offending statement is a simple primary-key lookup, and the only query-plan-level anomaly is report_rollup() at 12:32-12:35, which preceded the incident by ~10 minutes and was not repeated in the window. The causal link via Redis/cache is inferred, not directly measured.

hypotheses.description: Enabling feature.profile_v2_cache (12:10) inflated cached profile payloads ~4.1x, causing cache pressure and misses that push profile reads onto Postgres, saturating CPU/connections and causing slow user-profile queries and timeouts. Mechanism: Larger payloads reduce effective cache capacity/hit rate; misses fall back to SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=$1 against Postgres; DB CPU and connection utilisation climb; user-service queries exceed the 2000ms timeout, producing errors and p95 latency increase.

hypotheses.description: Heavy analytical/maintenance work on Postgres (report_rollup() and autovacuum on public.orders) consumed CPU and I/O, slowing point lookups on users. Mechanism: Long-running report_rollup() executions and autovacuum create CPU/IO contention; user lookups queue behind it, causing latency and timeouts.

probable_root_cause.description: Enabling feature.profile_v2_cache (12:10) inflated cached profile payloads ~4.1x, causing cache pressure and misses that push profile reads onto Postgres, saturating CPU/connections and causing slow user-profile queries and timeouts.
probable_root_cause.label: MOST PROBABLE EXPLANATION (INFERENCE, not confirmed)

root_cause_statement: MOST PROBABLE EXPLANATION (INFERENCE, not confirmed): configuration_regression in user-service - Enabling feature.profile_v2_cache (12:10) inflated cached profile payloads ~4.1x, causing cache pressure and misses that push profile reads onto Postgres, saturating CPU/connections and causing slow user-profile queries and timeouts.
corrective_actions: Roll back feature.profile_v2_cache to false (OPS-2229) and confirm Postgres CPU and user-service p95 recover
Once rolled back, verify that DB CPU returns to the ~35% baseline
Review report_rollup() scheduling to confirm it is not overlapping peak hours
preventive_actions: Gate feature flags that change cached payload size behind a canary and a cache-capacity check
Add a pre-change review for flags that change payload size or cache behaviour
Add cache-size and eviction budget tests to the flag rollout checklist
monitoring_recommendations: Alert on Redis/user-service cache hit rate and evictions (not currently collected)
Alert on cache-miss fallback rate to the DB
Alert on Postgres statement durations above 1s for users queries
Track user-service timeout_rate and p95 latency against the DB CPU
limitations: Causal link between the flag change and DB load is inferred from timing and log messages, not verified by a controlled test
Historical incident similarity is only an analogy
The 35-minute gap between the flag change (12:10) and the onset (12:45) is not fully explained
[agent-reported gap] No cache_hit_rate for user-service (metric not collected) and no Redis telemetry
[agent-reported gap] No pg_stat_activity or pg_stat_statements data to attribute CPU to specific queries
[agent-reported gap] No logs of report_rollup after 12:35 to rule it in or out for the 12:45+ window
[agent-reported gap] Log output is sampled/truncated (2 records omitted), so exact miss volumes are unknown
Confidence values are rule-based evidence-strength scores, not calibrated probabilities.
conclusion: The most likely root cause is the profile_v2_cache feature flag enabled at 12:10, which increased cached payload size ~4x and led to cache misses falling back to Postgres, driving CPU saturation and user-service timeouts from ~12:45. The bad-query theory is not well supported: the slow statement is a simple PK lookup, and report_rollup ran before the CPU rise. The cache-to-DB causal link is plausible and temporally ordered but not directly measured, because Redis and cache hit telemetry are missing. Confidence is moderate.
